attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own newsletter post.

semantics.note: It keeps the firm 'predominantly OpenAI compute' claim and the hedged 'maybe $8B at best' remainder. The pejorative framing is correctly left out.

contract.note: Reading 'predominantly' as a majority and taking the latest quarter before the post (FY26 Q3) is an ordinary, fair reading. Treating the hedged $8B as an estimate rather than a ceiling is correct.

evidence.note: Microsoft disclosure confirms the $37B+ AI ARR total. It gives no OpenAI or Copilot breakdown.

reviews.rationale: The only usable evidence confirms the $37B total. No same-basis breakdown shows OpenAI compute's share or that Copilot makes up the remainder. Key sources (Bloomberg Law, 10-K) were inaccessible, so the composition claim cannot be settled from the packet.

attribution.note: Zitron's own forecast in his own post.

semantics.note: 'I expect' is an unqualified expectation, so this is a scored forecast. 'Oinking about' is fairly rendered as hype. No deadline was stated.

contract.note: Reading 'oinking' as enthusiastic or promotional coverage, as opposed to critical coverage, is a fair ordinary reading. Whether a 'wave' happened depends on qualitative judgments of prominence and tone.

evidence.note: One BI Germany article frames loops as AI's big current topic. This is uptake by one outlet, not a cross-outlet wave.
O'Reilly reposts a practitioner essay that is hedged and skeptical. It is not independent journalism.
A republished practitioner post describes a peak hype cycle, mostly among engineers and at a conference rather than among journalists.
The Register covers loops as a buzzword but critically. Skeptical coverage does not refute an undated forecast.

reviews.rationale: Loops did get media uptake after June 8. But the packet shows mostly practitioner hype, one trend-framing news article and critical Register coverage. It does not clearly show a prominent wave of enthusiastic journalism across independent outlets, so the early-resolution rule is not met. With no deadline, the forecast stays open.

attribution.note: Zitron's own assertion, which he stresses as firm ('absolutely has to').

semantics.note: This is a firm necessity claim: the buildout is justified only if AI revenue exceeds $2T a year by 2030. The normalisation keeps the threshold, the scope and the 2030 horizon.

contract.note: Framing it as conditional necessity rather than a prediction of revenue is faithful. The demanding cost-reconciliation requirement fits a claim about what is needed.

evidence.note: Bain's 2025 estimate of about $2T needed by 2030 is a similar-scale consultant forecast. It is not an outcome, and it uses a different scope.

reviews.rationale: The deadline (end of 2030) is after the evaluation date, and no conclusive event is in the packet. Whether the buildout is financially viable (the antecedent) is unknown, and no realized revenue or cost data exist. The forecast cannot be scored yet.

semantics.note: It keeps the 'if half of the 190GW gets built' antecedent and the $875B figure. No horizon was stated.

contract.note: Tying the antecedent to the 190GW pipeline the speaker referenced is fair. Testing it against a cash break-even requires a financing model the speaker did not supply, so interpretation matters.

evidence.note: This identifies the 190GW announced cohort. It shows little under construction and does not establish that half is built.
The later outlook stresses delivery uncertainty. It gives no completion of half the cohort and no break-even estimate.

reviews.rationale: The antecedent (half of the 190GW pipeline operational) is not established, and the packet suggests it is far from met. There are no cohort-level financial records to test the $875B requirement. A conditional with an unmet or unknown antecedent is not scored.
